title: stutter-replay-cheat-sheet
content:
Quick notes + commands to reproduce intermittent streaming stutter / partial-frame hangs. Personal scratchpad — messy. Goal: capture a minimal, repeatable repro I can hand to SRE or paste into a PR.

Background/context
- Symptoms: client gets initial tokens, then a long pause (~2-30s) while server still generating. Eventually more tokens arrive as a burst (chunks concatenated) or stream resets. Sometimes connection resets with ECONNRESET.
- Hit list of suspects: ingress proxy buffering, TLS reneg, keepalive timeouts, server-side output buffer/backpressure, continuous-batching/kvcache flush, client-side read semantics.
- Observed headers often: Transfer-Encoding: chunked OR content-length absent (SSE). Occasionally intermediaries inject Content-Length=0 (??).

Important logs (snippets)
- client: "ERR_STREAM_RESET: remote peer closed stream while reading"
- server stderr (runtime): "kv_cache: eviction pressure triggered, stall for 280ms"
- nginx ingress: "upstream timed out (110: Connection timed out) while reading response header from upstream" (but not always)

Repro approaches tried (ordered by how reliable they were)
1) curl streaming, check raw bytes\-
- command: curl -v --no-buffer -H "Accept: text/event-stream" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "https://host/api/v1/streams?model=redwood-13b"
- notes: --no-buffer is required to see chunking as it arrives. With --no-buffer I still saw pauses (no chunk headers for long period). With netcat (see 3) the same behavior visible.

2) Python aiohttp client (async)\-
- code: \n  import aiohttp, asyncio\n  async def fetch():\n    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as s:\n      async with s.get(url, headers=headers) as r:\n        async for line in r.content:\n          print(repr(line))\n- outcome: sometimes asyncio waits until a larger internal buffer fills before yielding. Changing to r.content.read(1) helps show per-byte arrival, confirming server sent smaller writes that Python buffered.

3) netcat / openssl s_client to capture exact raw stream\-
- command (http over TLS):\n  printf "GET /api/v1/streams?model=... HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: host\r\nAuthorization: Bearer $TOKEN\r\nAccept: text/event-stream\r\nConnection: keep-alive\r\n\r\n" | openssl s_client -quiet -connect host:443 -ign_eof > raw.out
- outcome: raw.out shows chunk-length headers present and server does small chunk writes, but there are long gaps where no TCP segments transmitted.

4) go client that force-reads per byte (useful to rule out client buffering)\-
- gist of code: use net/http Client, resp.Body.Read(make([]byte,1)) in loop; print timestamps when bytes arrive.
- result: identical bursts/timing to openssl capture => server or network/intermediate.

5) tcpdump + wireshark to see packet pattern\-
- command: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w sse-repro.pcap host <client-ip> and port 443
- observation: during the pause period there are zero-to-no application data packets (pure ack) for 6-12s, then several small packets with PSH set arrive. Suggests server not sending rather than network dropping packets.

6) disable proxy (bypass nginx LB)\-
- result: significantly reduced pauses. When bypassed direct-to-backend, streaming becomes smoother. Points at ingress being involved. But not a full root cause — sometimes bypass still has smaller stutters.

Specific experiments to isolate backpressure sources
- Injected a 5ms sleep after every chunk write in the runtime to simulate a slow generator: reproduced identical behaviour on ingress (i.e., pause->burst).
- Replaced runtime small writes with a single write combining many tokens: pause disappears (because server writes fewer, larger frames).
- Set server socket TCP_NODELAY=1: no meaningful change (we already had small chunks delivered).

Hypotheses (ranked)
1) Ingress (nginx/ALB) buffering and heuristics: if it aggregates small writes to achieve Nagle-like behavior internally, it can create pauses. ALBs sometimes buffer until a content-length or a minimum flush size. Evidence: bypass makes it better.
2) Server-side output queue/backpressure: when internal request queue fills (batching + kv eviction), server stalls generation loop. Logs show kv_cache eviction spikes. Might be related, but tcpdump suggests there are no outgoing packets during pause. If server was blocking on write, it would still attempt to write to socket (but kernel buffer full). Hard to conclude.
3) TLS renegotiation / keepalive threshold at LB causing intermittent stalls — less likely given tcpdump showing server data bursts align with generation bursts.

Quick reproducer commands (to share)
- Minimal curl streaming test (use --no-buffer):\n  curl -v --no-buffer -H "Accept: text/event-stream" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "https://$HOST/stream?model=redwood-13b" 2>&1 | sed -u 's/\r//' | ts '%H:%M:%.S' > curl-stream.log
- Raw TLS capture (to show chunk boundaries):\n  printf "GET /stream?model=redwood-13b HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: $HOST\r\nAuthorization: Bearer $TOKEN\r\nAccept: text/event-stream\r\nConnection: keep-alive\r\n\r\n" | openssl s_client -quiet -connect $HOST:443 -servername $HOST > raw-tls.out
- Go tiny client (timestamps per byte) (paste to gist):\n  // make 1-byte buffer reads; print time.Now().UnixNano() on each non-zero read
- tcpdump for correlation: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w sse-debug.pcap host $HOST and port 443

Things to try next (TODO)
- Run nginx with proxy_buffering off and proxy_request_buffering off for this route (dev ingress). Compare latency traces.
- Try ALB vs NLB (layer 4) to confirm HTTP-level buffering effect.
- Add logging in runtime right before write() syscalls to see when the runtime attempts to send bytes. If runtime attempts but write blocks/returns EWOULDBLOCK, we know kernel buffer saturated.
- Compare with and without TLS (run HTTP on internal port) to rule out TLS stack buffering.
- Increase kv cache watermark to reduce eviction pressure; see if pause frequency changes.

Notes-to-self / gotchas
- Python and some HTTP libs buffer data internally. When capturing client-side, use raw sockets or read one byte at a time to avoid false negatives.
- curl --no-buffer helps but still does some processing; openssl s_client is the most truthful for TLS streams.
- If proxy adds gzip or other filters, small writes can be coalesced.

Possible quick mitigation for customers
- Zonally route streaming traffic to NLB (TCP passthrough) or ensure proxy has proxy_buffering off for streaming endpoints.
- Serve SSE over HTTP/2 event-stream? Might be worse (buffering) depending on intermediary. Needs testing.

Short raw timeline example (from tcpdump + logs)
- 12:01:05.123 -> initial small chunk (20 bytes) arrives to client.
- 12:01:05.124 -> client ACK.
- 12:01:07.5 -> no data for ~2.4s (no data packets).
- 12:01:07.6 -> server logs: "generation: sent token 64" (so generation continued).
- 12:01:07.6 -> at 12:01:07.655 several small packets arrive back-to-back with token 64..72 (burst).

Scratch hypotheses for PR description
- "Ingress buffer heuristic periodically aggregates small writes causing perceived stall. We recommend disabling proxy_buffering on streaming endpoints and/or using a TCP-level load balancer for streams. Server should also ensure write() flush on each token where possible and increase internal socket buffer if needed."

Next steps to hand-off
- Create test page on staging with configurable chunk-size and write-delay so SRE can toggle proxy settings and confirm.
- Collect full packet capture + server write-time logs from a timeline where pause observed and attach to Jira (LIN-3421).

Random notes / todo
- Add a small Go binary to repo: tools/stream-repro (1B writes with var delay)
- Check nginx versions for upstream_keepalive bug reported in 2024 that caused re-aggregation of buffered chunks
- Talk to infra about toggling ALB vs NLB for 10% of traffic to validate.

End of scratchpad.

-- riley
